howto.name: Meet the basic requirements
howto.text: Be at least 18 with a high school diploma or equivalent and a U.S. Social Security number.

howto.name: Complete the 63-hour pre-license course
howto.text: Finish Florida's state-approved 63-hour sales associate pre-license course and pass its end-of-course exam.

howto.name: Get fingerprinted
howto.text: Submit electronic fingerprints through a state-approved vendor for your background check.

howto.name: Apply to the DBPR
howto.text: Apply to the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation and receive your exam authorization.

howto.name: Pass the Florida state exam
howto.text: Pass the 100-question Florida sales associate exam (75% or higher) at a Pearson VUE testing center.

howto.name: Activate your license under a broker
howto.text: Join a licensed Florida broker, such as Adams, Cameron & Co., to activate your license and start working.

South Daytona is a small, established city on the mainland side of the Halifax River, sitting directly south of Daytona Beach and just north of Port Orange. Here’s exactly how to get licensed, and what the local market looks like for a new agent.

How do you get a real estate license in South Daytona?

You earn the Florida real estate sales associate license, valid statewide. There is no separate South Daytona license. Be 18+ with a high school diploma, complete the 63-hour pre-license course, get fingerprinted, apply to the DBPR, pass the state exam (75% to pass), and activate under a broker. Most people finish in two to four months. Full detail is in our Florida licensing guide.

Is South Daytona a good market for a new real estate agent?

Yes, and it’s worth understanding on its own terms rather than lumping it in with its bigger neighbors. South Daytona is a small, affordable, centrally located community of about 13,800 people, largely residential, on the mainland side of the Halifax River rather than the beachside. That affordability, relative to the wider county, tends to draw first-time buyers and people who want an easy, central location between Daytona Beach and Port Orange without paying beachside prices. Across Volusia County, roughly 900 homes sell each month at about a $343,000 median, and a new agent working South Daytona is working inside that same steady county-wide demand.

From Blake to South Daytona: a century of quiet growth

South Daytona wasn’t always South Daytona. For decades it was the town of Blake, named after Alpheus P. Blake, a businessman from Boston who established a post office here in 1878. Blake grew as a quiet residential settlement on the mainland side of the Halifax River, far enough from Daytona Beach to stay its own place, but close enough to benefit from regional growth. The city incorporated as South Daytona on June 18, 1951, marking a deliberate identity shift: it wasn’t trying to be a beach destination, but rather a stable, affordable, residential alternative to the tourist towns on either side. That founding ethos has stuck for 75 years. For an agent, that history means working in a place where buyers have usually chosen South Daytona deliberately, for that quiet, established residential character, not a beach vacation rental or seasonal property.

South Daytona’s single-family residential character

More than half of South Daytona’s housing stock is single-family detached homes, which shapes every part of the market. This isn’t a condo market like the beach, and it isn’t dense multifamily development like some inland urban centers. It’s neighborhoods of single-family homes, mostly built before and just after the 1951 incorporation, meaning many carry the solidity and larger lot sizes of mid-20th-century residential development. This composition has real consequences for an agent: your buyers are likely families or retirees looking for a home and a yard, not investors looking to flip condos or landlords building rental portfolios. That’s a simpler, longer-holding buyer profile, and it means building knowledge of neighborhood walkability, school districts, and property condition matters more than speculative trends.

Buying power and steady demographics in South Daytona

South Daytona’s median household income of roughly $56,500 and a median age around 48 years paint a clear picture of its buyer base. This is a place where established households and retirees have put down root, and where first-time buyers on ordinary incomes can still afford a home. The recent median sale price hovers around $329,000, which is well within reach of dual-income families and significantly below the beachside markets five miles east. That affordability, held year after year, creates predictable demand: people stay here, they hold their homes longer, and the sales that do happen tend to be genuine life-stage moves, downsizing, relocating, starting out, rather than speculation or short-term flips. For a new agent, that stability is valuable. It means your pipeline isn’t as frenetic as a hot-market beach town, but it’s also more reliable.

South Daytona is growing quietly, off the tourist track

Over the past few years, South Daytona has grown meaningfully, adding roughly 1,400 people to its population since 2020, a 10.75% increase, even as it remains intentionally small. That growth happens outside the tourism and seasonal churn that defines Daytona Beach proper, which means new residents are people choosing to live here, not tourists choosing to visit. Long-term home appreciation in South Daytona has been strong, roughly 149% over the past ten years, reflecting both the regional Volusia County market and South Daytona’s own steady residential appeal. For a new agent, that combination matters: there’s real buyer demand, reliable inventory, and genuine equity growth, but without the beach-market hysteria or the seasonal volatility. You’re competing on service and knowledge, not just on market temperature.

Does the brokerage you start with matter?

More than the town you pick. Your license must be held by a broker, and that brokerage decides your training, tools, and support in the make-or-break first year. A recognized local name carries real weight. Sellers trust it before you say a word.

Why start your real estate career with Adams, Cameron & Co.?

Adams, Cameron & Co. has been the area’s largest brokerage since 1963. South Daytona doesn’t have its own dedicated Adams, Cameron & Co. office, but the company’s Daytona Beach headquarters and its Port Orange office are both just minutes away, so hands-on support is never far. New agents get in-house marketing at no cost, seven-day non-competing manager support, structured training, and the global Leading Real Estate Companies of the World referral network.

What is your next step?

Read the licensing guide, go deeper on the town’s real story in our full history of South Daytona, then start a conversation with Adams, Cameron & Co. No pressure, just a clear picture of the path.
